newsitem.title: MONACO: SOCCER SHOWCASE-EXTREMES CLASH AS MONACO HOST MARSEILLE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-EXTREMES CLASH AS MONACO HOST MARSEILLE.

text.p: Extremes clash when quiet Monaco, the runaway league leaders, host turbulent Marseille in the French first division on Saturday.
Apart from both being on the Mediterranean coast, the two cities have little in common.
When one talks of Marseille, passion and controversy immediately come to mind, and not only because of its flamboyant soccer club.
Monaco, on the other hand, is ever so discrete and careful not to attract any unneeded attention.
Marseille, a busy town badly hit by unemployment, has a harbour with big, rusty ships while the only boats anchored off Monaco are spotless millionaires' yachts.
But the Marseille fans are not impressed. They even smile when reminded that Monaco won five league titles and as many domestic Cup trophies.
With eight titles and 10 Cup victories, including a triumph in the 1993 European Cup, Marseille are the greatest club in French soccer history.
"There's a real rivalry between Marseille and Paris but not with Monaco," said a keen Marseille fan. "Where is Monaco anyway? Is it in France?"
A few years ago, Monaco considered joining the Italian league.
Marseille, however, are rarely out of the media spotlight.
The match-rigging scandal which cost them their league title in 1993 and sent them to the second division was a national drama.
Heavy debts forced them to stay in the second division for two years.
Back with the best this season, they signed foreign stars such as German goalkeeper Andreas Koepke and Bulgarian midfielder Yordan Lechkov, hoping the glory days would soon return.
But they have failed to recapture their brilliant form and are currently 12th.
Since 1986 and prior to their enforced relegation over the 1993 bribery scandal, Marseille have never finished lower than sixth.

Marseille have yet to win away this season and face the prospect of becoming only the second team in the club's history to go through a season without an away victory, equalling the effort of the 1958/59 side.
"We will give our all to win in Monaco because we don't want to end the season without a single away win," said Lechkov.

More than anybody else, Patrick Blondeau knows the difference between Marseille and Monaco. Raised in a concrete block in the infamous northern suburbs of Marseille, the Monaco defender discovered an entirely new world when he joined the principality.
"When I was a kid in Marseille, I really loved soccer," he said. "When I arrived in Monaco, I found out it was all about business."
